answer: Harberger-taxed seats cap a farm's identities. Each of 10,000 fixed earning seats has a holder-declared price, taxed 2% per epoch, and must be sold to anyone paying it. Pricing a seat like ivory deters buyers but raises its tax, so quotes stay modest. A farm buys cheapest first: the 1st seat may cost 50 POA, the 1,000th over 900, plus tax on each. Each sale lands in a public mirror of the order book, so holders spot a spree and reprice. Random audits re-grade one job on 3% of seats, e.g. a trellis load estimate; failure forfeits the seat. Weakness: wealth still buys share, at rising cost.
